beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Pavan Majji, a backend software engineer. This is my final project, Cite the Line. When something breaks, the better question isn't how to fix it, but which log lines prove the cause.

show.event: corrects 'how do I fix it' → 'which log lines prove it'

props.text:
What caused this error,
and how do I fix it?

beats.motion_claim: The writer corrects the naive fix-it question into the real one.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. Root cause: the failure that started the problem. Source grounding: every claim points to the exact text it came from. A human gate: a point where the system hands a decision to a person.

terms.meaning: the failure that started the problem

beats.narration_text: When a backend service fails, engineers often paste the error into a chatbot and act on the answer, without checking it against the logs.

beats.narration_text: Cite the Line will read the logs from a failing service, name the likely cause, and point to the exact lines that prove it.

beats.narration_text: Why it matters: a wrong root cause sends a team to fix the wrong thing. An answer you can check against the log is one you can trust, or reject.

beats.narration_text: Others have tried this. Microsoft researchers built R C A Copilot, which predicts the root cause category of cloud incidents. On a year of Microsoft's own incidents, they report accuracy up to about seventy-seven percent.

beats.narration_text: Both scores come from data an outsider can't see or re-run. Mine will publish the incidents, the known answers, and every mistake, so anyone can check the score themselves.

beats.narration_text: Step one, the data. I'll build a small FastAPI service with a Postgres database, running in Docker.

beats.narration_text: Then I'll break it on purpose: a slowed database, a bad config, a failing dependency. Each break produces real logs with a known cause, so no private data is needed.

beats.narration_text: Step two, the agent loop. For each incident, it reads the logs, asks Claude Code for a diagnosis in a fixed format, checks it, records it, and moves on.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft ring with four stations: log page, 'Claude Code' box, checker slip with a check, and a record stack; a terracotta dot travels the ring once; a small 'constructed sketch' tag in the lower-right corner.

beats.narration_text: Its tools are limited. It can read log files, and nothing else. It never restarts, rolls back, or changes anything.

beats.narration_text: It stops on rules, not on the model's say-so: three runs per incident, and at most one retry when an answer breaks the format.

beats.narration_text: And there's a human gate. Any diagnosis marked not enough evidence, or rejected by the checker, goes to an engineer, who makes the call.

beats.narration_text: Do I have what I need? Claude Code through my university seat, so no paid credits. My laptop for compute. Docker and Python, which I already use. No new accounts.

beats.narration_text: To test it, I'll create about ten incidents with known causes, including hard ones, where the loudest error isn't the real cause, and ones with no clear answer.

beats.narration_text: Three checks. Every cited line must exist in the log; one invented line counts as a failure. The cause must match the known answer. And on the no-answer cases, it must decline instead of guessing.

beats.narration_text: The baseline: a simple keyword script, scored on the same incidents. If Claude can't beat it, the tool didn't work, or my test was too easy. Either way, I'll publish the result.
